segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is impossible for stumbling blocks not to come, but woe to the one through whom they come!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Be on your guard. If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he turns back, forgive him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if he sins against you seven times in a day and seven times comes back to you saying, ‘I turn back,’ you must forgive him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The apostles said to the Lord,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Increase our faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Lord said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which of you who has a slave plowing or tending sheep will say to him when he comes in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at the table’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Will he not say to him instead, ‘Prepare something for my dinner, tie up your tunic and serve me while I eat and drink, and after that you may eat and drink’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He does not thank the slave for doing what was commanded, does he?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you also, when you have done everything that was commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy slaves; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the way to Jerusalem, he was passing between Samaria and Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was entering a village, ten men with a skin disease met him. They stood at a distance

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and raised their voices, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw them, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go and show yourselves to the priests.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as they went, they were cleansed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of them, seeing that he had been healed, returned, glorifying God in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and fell on his face at the feet of Jesus, thanking him. And he was a Samaritan.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus responded,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Were not the ten cleansed? Where are the nine?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Was no one found returning to give glory to God except this foreigner?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up and go on your way; your faith has saved you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of God is not coming in a way that can be observed,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: nor will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or ‘There!’ For look, the kingdom of God is among you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Days will come when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They will say to you, ‘Look, there! Look, here!’ Do not go off or chase after them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For just as lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And just as it was in the days of Noah, so it will be also in the days of the Son of Man:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: they were eating, drinking, marrying, being given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot: they were eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but on the day Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It will be just the same on the day the Son of Man is revealed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: On that day, anyone on the roof whose belongings are in the house must not go down to take them, and likewise anyone in the field must not turn to what is behind.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Remember Lot’s wife.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever seeks to secure his life will lose it, but whoever loses it will keep it alive.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, on that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: There will be two women grinding together: one will be taken and the other left.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They responded and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where, Lord?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Where the body is, there the vultures too will gather.”

notes.note: The Greek verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Repent” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, so this translation uses “turn back.” Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

The Greek word means a person owned by a master, not a hired worker, and the parable depends on that: a slave who does what he is told has earned no special thanks. The KJV, ESV and NIV have “servant”; the NRSV, NASB and NET have “slave.”

The Greek adjective ordinarily means “useless” or “worthless.” Here it is usually taken as a statement of modesty: slaves who have only done their duty have no claim to special credit. Translations vary among “unprofitable,” “unworthy” and “worthless”; some scholars propose “to whom nothing is owed,” which fits the parable but is less certain as a meaning of the word.

notes.traditional: through the midst of Samaria and Galilee
notes.note: The Greek phrase could mean “through the middle of Samaria and Galilee” or “along the border between” them. Samaria lies south of Galilee, so a route along the border region makes better geographical sense for someone heading to Jerusalem, and it would explain a group that includes both Jews and a Samaritan. The exact route Luke has in mind is debated.

The Greek word names someone with the condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why the men are “cleansed.” “Leper” today means a person with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers,” usually with a footnote making this point; the traditional word does convey the severity and social exclusion involved.

Under Leviticus 13–14 a person with this condition lived apart from the community, which is why the men stand at a distance, and could return only after a priest had examined them and declared them clean. Jesus sends them for that inspection before any change is visible; the cleansing comes as they go.

Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel and kept the Law of Moses, but Jews regarded them as outsiders. The Greek word used here occurs only this once in the New Testament; it is the term used on the inscription in the Jerusalem temple that warned non-Jews not to enter the inner courts.

The Greek verb means both “heal” and “save,” and many translations have “made you well” here. But all ten were cleansed and only this man is told this, so the saying probably points to more than the cure. The identical sentence closes other scenes in Luke (7:50; 8:48; 18:42).

The Greek preposition can mean “within” or “among, in the midst of.” “Within you” is the older English rendering, but Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and does not elsewhere describe the kingdom as an inner state, so most recent translations and scholars prefer “among you” or “in your midst.” A third proposal, “within your reach,” also has scholarly support.

Verse 36 (“Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left”) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not part of the Greek text translated here. It was probably added by copyists from Matthew 24:40. The traditional verse numbers are kept, so the chapter moves from verse 35 to verse 37.

The Greek word normally means “eagle,” and the KJV has “eagles.” Ancient writers did not always distinguish eagles from vultures, and birds gathering at a body are carrion birds, so most modern translations have “vultures.” Some interpreters see an allusion to the eagle standards of the Roman legions; this is possible but uncertain.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translations split between “slave” and “servant,” which changes how readers hear parables and Paul’s self-descriptions.
The verb covers both healing and salvation, and the recurring formula “your faith has saved you” is rendered inconsistently across healing stories.
Whether to render “brother,” “brother or sister” or “fellow believer” where the reference is generic needs one policy across the Gospels and letters.
A title for Jesus found only in Luke that must be kept distinct from the renderings of κύριος, διδάσκαλος and ῥαββί.
For skin disease the verb is ritual as well as physical, and translations vary between “cleanse,” “make clean” and “heal” across the Gospels.
